2026-10-03|Half Oceanman.headline: You finished the 5 km Half Oceanman swim in 2:33:18 (2:57/100 m), beating your training-pace prediction of 2:29:55 by only 3½ minutes but landing 28 minutes short of your 2:05 target — a result that is hard to separate from a 6-week build in which only 18% of planned sessions were completed and race-week sleep averaged just 4.5 hours.
went_well: You edged your naive training-pace prediction (2:33:18 vs 2:29:55), meaning race-day conditions or adrenaline offset at least some of the fitness deficit — a modest but real positive given the preparation.

Your race pace of 2:57/100 m was 3 seconds per 100 m faster than your average training pace of 3:00/100 m (speed gain of +2% in real terms, though logged as -2% — worth verifying the sign), showing you can lift slightly above training speed on race day.
Taper execution was reasonable: a 47% load reduction in race week sits within the normal 40–60% range, so at least the final week was managed sensibly despite the chaotic wider build.
to_improve: Volume and consistency were the clearest structural problem: 7 of 40 planned sessions completed (18%) across 6 weeks, with only 5.9 km total swim training for a 5 km race — your longest single session was 2.0 km, just 40% of race distance. You effectively went into a 5 km event having never swum beyond 40% of that distance in training.

Race-week sleep of 4.5 hours against a baseline of 5.8 hours is a meaningful drop; while one data point cannot prove it cost you time, chronic sleep restriction is consistently associated with impaired endurance performance and perceived effort — worth actively protecting in future race weeks.

The 28-minute gap between actual (2:33:18) and target (2:05:00) reflects a target that required 2:30/100 m pace — 27 seconds per 100 m faster than your recent training average of 3:00/100 m. Future targets should be anchored to demonstrated training paces, not aspirational ones, so race-week decisions are based on realistic benchmarks.
next_race: The Treviso 10K Tiramisu Run is tomorrow (2026-10-11), so training changes are irrelevant — treat today as full rest, prioritise eating and hydrating well, and aim for the best sleep you can manage tonight; do not attempt any shake-out effort that adds fatigue.

Set a conservative pace target for tomorrow based on recent run training data, not ambition — your body has just completed a 5 km open-water swim race and is carrying accumulated fatigue from a low-compliance build.

Use the 120 days to the February marathon as a genuine reset: establish a sustainable weekly session floor (even 2–3 consistent sessions per week would be a major improvement on 18% compliance) rather than loading a high planned volume you cannot hit.
